clinicalPearls: Anomalous mitral arcade, or hammock valve, is a rare congenital dysplasia in which the papillary muscles attach directly to the leaflet free edge through a bridging band of fibrous tissue, obliterating the normal chordae.
It causes mixed mitral dysfunction, with regurgitation from restricted coaptation and stenosis from limited leaflet opening.
It often forms part of the congenital mitral dysplasia spectrum and may coexist with parachute valve, supravalvar mitral ring and subaortic stenosis within Shone complex.
Echocardiography shows papillary muscles displaced towards the annulus with a hammock-like subvalvar apparatus and thickened, immobile leaflet edges.
It is distinguished from parachute mitral valve, in which chordae converge on a single papillary muscle, whereas the arcade shows direct muscular or fibrous attachment to the leaflet margin.
Because chordal shortening tethers the leaflet tips while the body may still billow, the appearance should not be mistaken for prolapse.
Surgical repair is difficult owing to the deficient subvalvar apparatus, and valve replacement is sometimes required.
reference.pathophysiology: The lesion results from abnormal development of the mitral tension apparatus in which the interchordal spaces fail to form. The papillary muscles insert directly onto the free margin of the anterior leaflet, or a continuous fibrous arcade bridges the papillary muscle tips along the leaflet edge, so that discrete chordae are effectively absent. The resulting tethering restricts leaflet excursion, producing regurgitation through failure of coaptation and stenosis through limited diastolic opening. The abnormality lies within the wider spectrum of congenital mitral valve dysplasia and commonly accompanies other left-heart obstructive lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital mitral stenosis with supravalvar mitral ring
Cleft mitral valve or atrioventricular septal defect
Ischaemic or dysplastic papillary muscle dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with focused subvalvar apparatus imaging
Cardiac catheterisation with transvalvar pressure measurement
Screening for associated Shone-complex left-heart obstructive lesions
redFlags: Heart failure or pulmonary oedema from severe mitral dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on severity and associated lesions; mild disease may remain stable for years, but significant mixed mitral disease often needs repair or replacement, and the deficient subvalvar apparatus makes durable repair difficult.
pitfalls: Confusing arcade with parachute valve or rheumatic disease
Mistaking tethered leaflet tips with a billowing body for prolapse
Underestimating the stenosis component when regurgitation dominates the clinical picture
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Definitive management is surgical: repair of the dysplastic subvalvar apparatus where anatomy allows, or mitral valve replacement when the deficient chordal support precludes durable repair
Medical control of pulmonary congestion and heart failure with diuretics and afterload reduction ahead of surgery
Precise echocardiographic delineation of papillary muscles, chordae and leaflets to define the mixed stenosis and regurgitation mechanism and distinguish it from parachute valve and prolapse
Screen for and manage associated Shone-complex lesions including parachute valve, supravalvar mitral ring and subaortic or aortic obstruction
Monitor for and treat pulmonary hypertension and right heart strain
Nutritional support for infants with failure to thrive and feeding difficulty
Paediatric cardiology and congenital cardiac surgical follow-up for residual or recurrent valve dysfunction
